title: Grade inflation, or better teaching?

turns.speaker: Struan
turns.text: A third of the cohort got a first this year. When I graduated it was about seven per cent.

turns.speaker: Nate
turns.text: The obvious reply is that teaching improved and students work harder because they're paying.

turns.speaker: Priyanka
turns.text: Some of that is real. Contact hours and feedback genuinely are better than they were in the eighties.

turns.speaker: Priyanka
turns.text: No. And the entry qualifications of the same cohort didn't rise anywhere near proportionally, which is the comparison that matters.

turns.speaker: Nate
turns.text: The mechanism isn't dishonesty, though. It's a thousand reasonable decisions. Round up a borderline case, drop the worst module, mark the coursework generously.

turns.speaker: Struan
turns.text: And every one of those is defensible on its own.

turns.speaker: Struan
turns.text: It's only the aggregate over twenty years that looks absurd.

turns.speaker: Priyanka
turns.text: There's a league table effect too. Good degree outcomes are a ranking metric, so the institution benefits from its own generosity.

turns.speaker: Nate
turns.text: Who's actually harmed? That's the question I keep coming back to.

turns.speaker: Priyanka
turns.text: The strong students, mostly. If a third have the top grade it stops telling an employer anything, so employers fall back on which university you went to.

turns.speaker: Struan
turns.text: Which advantages exactly the people who were already advantaged.

turns.speaker: Nate
turns.text: So the inflation is egalitarian in appearance and the opposite in effect.

points: A third of a cohort achieved first-class degrees, against about seven per cent a generation ago.
Priyanka accepts teaching and feedback genuinely improved, but not proportionally, and entry qualifications did not rise comparably.
Nate describes the mechanism as an accumulation of individually defensible decisions rather than dishonesty.
League tables reward good degree outcomes, so institutions benefit from their own generosity.
Priyanka argues strong students are harmed, because a common top grade stops signalling anything.
Employers then fall back on institutional reputation, which advantages those already advantaged, making the effect the opposite of egalitarian.
